scenes.title: Managed Relational Databases
scenes.narration: Managed relational databases like Amazon RDS and Cloud SQL run engines such as PostgreSQL and MySQL for you, handling backups, patching, and failover.

scenes.title: What the Provider Handles
bullets: Automated backups and point-in-time recovery protect you from data loss.
Patching and minor version upgrades happen without you touching a server.
Multi-AZ deployments provide automatic failover to a standby if the primary fails.
scenes.narration: A managed database takes over the operational chores that used to consume database administrators. Automated backups and point-in-time recovery guard against mistakes and corruption. The provider patches the engine for you, and a multi-AZ standby fails over automatically when the primary goes down.

scenes.title: Self-Managed vs. Managed
scenes.narration: Running a database yourself on a VM gives total control but demands constant care: installing, patching, and configuring backups. A managed service trades some of that control for dramatically less operational toil. For most teams, the time saved far outweighs the flexibility given up.

scenes.title: How Failover Works
steps: DNS flips to the promoted standby
scenes.narration: In a multi-AZ setup the primary instance serves traffic while a standby copies every change synchronously. If the primary fails, the service promotes the standby and repoints the database endpoint to it. Your application reconnects to the same address, often with only a brief interruption.

scenes.title: Creating an RDS Instance
scenes.code:
aws rds create-db-instance \
  --db-instance-identifier analytics-db \
  --engine postgres \
  --db-instance-class db.m6g.large \
  --allocated-storage 100 \
  --multi-az \
  --master-username admin
scenes.narration: This command provisions a managed PostgreSQL database in a single step. The engine flag chooses the database type, the instance class sizes the compute, and allocated-storage sets the disk. Adding the multi-az flag turns on the automatic failover standby, giving you high availability from the moment it launches.

scenes.text: Managed relational databases hand off backups, patching, and failover so you focus on schema and queries — reach for them unless you truly need custom control.
scenes.narration: Managed relational databases remove most database administration work, letting you concentrate on data modeling and queries. Unless a workload demands unusual engine tuning, the managed option is almost always the pragmatic choice.
